title: Motorized DNA Double Helix Model
concept: DNA structure, base pairing and genetic information
materials: two flexible wires or rods for the strands
coloured straws, beads or small foam pieces for the base pairs
materialsText: Cardboard or plywood base; DC geared motor (3–6 V); battery holder and batteries; on/off switch; connecting wires; two flexible wires or rods for the strands; coloured straws, beads or small foam pieces for the base pairs; glue; labels
speech: Good morning. This model shows the double-helix structure of DNA, the molecule that carries genetic information in living things. The two twisting strands are joined by pairs of bases: adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine. The small motor slowly rotates the model so that we can see the twisted shape more clearly. DNA contains instructions that help organisms grow, function and pass characteristics from one generation to the next.
note: Use a low-voltage geared motor and secure the rotating structure so it cannot wobble or catch fingers.

title: Working Escalator Model
concept: Continuous motion, gears, belts and energy conversion
materials: cardboard step pieces or a small linked-step chain
wooden skewers or metal rods for axles
rubber belt or suitable looped chain
materialsText: Corrugated cardboard or foam board; cardboard step pieces or a small linked-step chain; two rollers or pulleys; DC geared motor; battery holder and batteries; switch; wooden skewers or metal rods for axles; rubber belt or suitable looped chain; glue; cutter; paint or labels
speech: This is a small working model of an escalator, which is used to move people between different floor levels. The motor turns a belt or chain mechanism that carries the steps around a continuous path. The steps are guided so that they remain nearly horizontal while moving along the sloping section. This model demonstrates how electrical energy is converted into mechanical motion and how machines make transport easier in places such as shopping centres and railway stations.
note: Keep fingers away from the moving belt, rollers and step mechanism. A hand-operated version can be used if a motorised mechanism is difficult to build.

title: Hologram Illusion Display
concept: Reflection of light and optical illusion
materials: Clear acrylic or transparent plastic sheet
materialsText: Clear acrylic or transparent plastic sheet; cardboard or foam-board enclosure; smartphone or tablet; suitable hologram/illusion video; black chart paper; ruler; tape; glue; cutter; optional LED lighting
speech: This project creates a hologram-like visual illusion using light and a transparent surface. A specially prepared video is shown on a phone, and the image is reflected by the clear plastic or acrylic arrangement so that it appears to float inside the display. It is an optical illusion rather than a true hologram, but it helps us understand how reflection and viewing angle can create a three-dimensional-looking image. The dark background makes the reflected image easier to see.
note: Call it a hologram illusion or Pepper’s-Ghost-style display, not a true 3D hologram. The exact sheet arrangement should match the video and design being used.

title: Human Body and Brain Model
concept: Human organs, body systems and brain structure
materials: Large cardboard, plywood or foam-board base
coloured yarn, string or flexible tubing for vessels
materialsText: Large cardboard, plywood or foam-board base; thermocol/foam sheet or papier-mâché; modelling clay; paints and brushes; coloured yarn, string or flexible tubing for vessels; printed brain/organ diagrams; labels; glue; scissors; markers
speech: This model introduces the major organs of the human body and shows where they are located. The brain is the control centre of the nervous system: it receives information, processes it and helps coordinate our actions and body functions. Other organs, such as the heart and lungs, work together to keep the body alive. By looking at the model, we can learn how different organs have different jobs but depend on one another.
note: Label only the organs and brain parts that students can correctly identify and explain.

title: Hydraulic JCB Excavator
concept: Pascal’s law and hydraulic machines
materials: wooden skewers or bolts for pivots
materialsText: Cardboard, plywood or foam-board base; ice-cream sticks or wooden strips; 4–6 large syringes; flexible plastic tubes; water; wooden skewers or bolts for pivots; small scoop/bucket; glue or hot glue; tape; cutter; optional paint
speech: This is a model of a hydraulic excavator. It uses syringes connected by tubes filled with water. When we push one syringe, pressure is transmitted through the liquid and moves another syringe, which makes the arm or bucket move. This demonstrates Pascal’s law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted through the liquid. Hydraulic machines use this principle to lift and move heavy loads.
note: Fill the paired syringe-and-tube circuits with water and remove as much trapped air as possible. Keep the load light and supervise cutting and hot-glue work.

title: Kaleidoscope
concept: Multiple reflection of light
materials: three narrow mirror strips or reflective acrylic strips
materialsText: Cardboard tube; three narrow mirror strips or reflective acrylic strips; transparent plastic discs; small coloured beads or sequins; translucent/frosted plastic or tracing paper; cardboard end caps; decorative paper; tape; glue; scissors
speech: A kaleidoscope produces beautiful patterns using the principle of multiple reflection. Three reflective strips are arranged inside the tube to form a triangular arrangement. Light enters from one end and reflects repeatedly between the mirrors, creating a symmetrical pattern. When we rotate the kaleidoscope, the coloured pieces move and a new pattern appears.
note: Cover mirror edges carefully so that no sharp edges are exposed.

title: Volcano Eruption Model
concept: Volcano structure and gas-producing reaction demonstration
materials: newspaper and papier-mâché or modelling clay
materialsText: Cardboard or plywood base; small plastic bottle; newspaper and papier-mâché or modelling clay; paints; baking soda; vinegar; a little dishwashing liquid; red/orange food colour; tray; spoon and measuring cup
speech: This model represents a volcano and shows how an eruption can send material down its sides. In our demonstration, baking soda reacts with vinegar and produces carbon dioxide gas. The gas creates bubbles and pushes the coloured foam out of the opening. This is a safe classroom simulation of an eruption, not the actual process inside a volcano, where hot magma, dissolved gases and pressure are involved.
note: Use small quantities on a tray under teacher supervision. The reaction is a classroom simulation; do not use flames, sealed containers or strong chemicals.

title: Map Explorer – Electrical Geography Quiz Board
concept: Geography recall and simple electric circuits
materials: Printed map (the pictured example is a map of Europe)
cardboard, foam board or plywood backing
materialsText: Printed map (the pictured example is a map of Europe); cardboard, foam board or plywood backing; metal brads/screws/contact points; country-name labels; insulated connecting wires; LED; suitable current-limiting resistor; low-voltage battery; buzzer (optional); switch; two insulated probe wires; glue and marker
speech: This is an interactive geography quiz board. One side shows a map and the other side has country names. The participant uses the two probes to match a country with its correct location. When the correct contacts are connected, the electric circuit is completed and the LED or buzzer gives a signal. The project combines map-reading skills with the basic idea of an electric circuit.
note: Use a low-voltage battery and a current-limiting resistor with the LED. Check the contact pairs carefully so only correct matches complete the circuit.

title: Molecular Structure Model
concept: Atoms, chemical elements and bonding
materials: Thermocol/foam balls or modelling clay in different colours
glue. Select a particular molecule and prepare the correct number and arrangement of atoms before building
materialsText: Thermocol/foam balls or modelling clay in different colours; toothpicks or short wooden/plastic rods; paints; cardboard or wooden base; labels; marker; glue. Select a particular molecule and prepare the correct number and arrangement of atoms before building
speech: This model represents a molecule, which is made when two or more atoms are joined by chemical bonds. The coloured balls represent different types of atoms, and the connecting rods represent bonds between them. The arrangement of atoms is important because it helps determine a substance’s properties. Our model is a simplified, enlarged representation that makes a very small structure easier to understand.
note: The pictured model does not identify a particular molecule. Students should choose a named molecule, then verify its formula and structure before labelling the model.

title: Simple Homopolar Motor
concept: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor
materials: bare copper wire that can be bent into the shown shape
materialsText: One AA battery; small neodymium disc magnet; bare copper wire that can be bent into the shown shape; optional small base or holder; wire cutters/pliers; eye protection for wire shaping
speech: This is a simple homopolar motor. When the copper wire touches the battery and the magnet, an electric current flows through the wire in a magnetic field. The interaction between the current and the magnetic field produces a force that makes the wire move around the battery. It is a simple demonstration of how electrical energy can be converted into motion.
note: Run it only for a few seconds at a time under close supervision. The wire can heat up because the arrangement draws a large current. Disconnect it immediately if the battery or wire becomes warm.

title: Newton’s Cradle
concept: Transfer of momentum and energy in collisions
materials: strong thin thread or fishing line
materialsText: Five equal-sized steel balls; strong thin thread or fishing line; wooden or cardboard frame; support rods; glue or screws; ruler; pliers; optional labels
speech: Newton’s cradle demonstrates what happens when balls collide. When we lift and release one ball, it strikes the row and the ball at the other end swings outward. The motion is explained by the transfer of momentum and energy through the collisions. In a real model, some energy is also lost as sound, heat and air resistance, so the balls gradually stop.
note: Use balls of similar size and mass, and suspend them at equal heights so they touch in a straight line.

title: Satellite Model
concept: Satellites, communication and solar power in space
materials: Small cardboard or foam-board box for the satellite body
blue card or mini solar cells for solar panels
ice-cream sticks or thin rods for antennae
materialsText: Small cardboard or foam-board box for the satellite body; blue card or mini solar cells for solar panels; aluminium foil; ice-cream sticks or thin rods for antennae; wires; optional small LED and battery; glue; paint; labels; display stand
speech: This model represents an artificial satellite that can travel around Earth. Satellites are used for communication, weather forecasting, navigation, scientific research and observing our planet. Many satellites use solar panels to convert sunlight into electrical energy for their instruments. The model shows some external parts of a satellite, including its main body, solar panels and antennae.
note: This is a display model unless a working radio or electronic function is added. Do not imply that the model demonstrates an actual orbit.

title: Solar System Model
concept: The Sun, planets and their order in the solar system
materials: Eight thermocol/foam balls in different sizes
string or wire for orbit paths
materialsText: Eight thermocol/foam balls in different sizes; large base board; paints and brushes; wooden skewers or wire supports; string or wire for orbit paths; labels; glue; optional LEDs, battery and switch
speech: This model shows the Sun and the eight planets of our solar system in their order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The planets travel around the Sun in separate orbits. The model helps us compare their order and approximate relative sizes, although the distances and sizes are not shown to the same scale.
note: Clearly label the planets. If the model uses lights or a motor, explain those as display features rather than as a scale representation of the real solar system.

title: Simple Refracting Telescope
concept: Refraction and magnification by lenses
materials: One convex objective lens with a longer focal length
one convex eyepiece lens with a shorter focal length
two cardboard tubes that slide inside one another
materialsText: One convex objective lens with a longer focal length; one convex eyepiece lens with a shorter focal length; two cardboard tubes that slide inside one another; lens holders; black paper; tape; glue; tripod or stable stand
speech: This is a simple refracting telescope. It uses lenses to collect light from a distant object and form an image that we can view through the eyepiece. The objective lens forms an image, and the eyepiece magnifies it for the observer. By sliding the tubes, we change the distance between the lenses to bring the image into focus.
note: Never point the telescope at the Sun. Direct sunlight through a telescope can cause permanent eye injury.

title: Wireless Power Transfer Demonstration
concept: Electromagnetic induction and energy transfer
materials: Transmitter coil and receiver coil made with insulated copper wire
receiver LED with suitable resistor or receiver module
materialsText: Transmitter coil and receiver coil made with insulated copper wire; low-voltage wireless-power oscillator/transmitter module; receiver LED with suitable resistor or receiver module; low-voltage battery or regulated supply; connecting wires; cardboard base; tape; labels
speech: This project demonstrates how electrical energy can be transferred between two coils without a direct wire connection. The transmitter circuit sends a changing current through its coil, producing a changing magnetic field. This changing field induces a voltage in the nearby receiver coil, which can light an LED. The distance and alignment between the coils affect how much energy is transferred.
note: Use a purpose-built low-voltage oscillator or wireless-power module. A coil connected directly to a battery produces no continuous changing magnetic field and can overheat.

title: Archimedes Screw Water Pump
concept: A rotating helical surface lifting water
materials: Transparent PVC pipe or clear tube
flexible plastic hose or spiral strip to form the screw
hand crank or low-speed geared motor
materialsText: Transparent PVC pipe or clear tube; flexible plastic hose or spiral strip to form the screw; central rod; hand crank or low-speed geared motor; support frame; two water containers; water; base board; glue or clamps
speech: This model demonstrates an Archimedes screw, a simple machine used to lift water from a lower level to a higher level. When the screw turns, pockets of water are carried upward along the spiral path inside the tube. The device has been used for irrigation and water movement. It shows how a rotating mechanism can move water without using a conventional pump impeller.
note: Keep the frame stable and use a slow hand crank or low-voltage geared motor. Prevent water from reaching electrical components.

title: Buzz Wire Game
concept: Electric circuits and electrical continuity
materials: Thick bare metal wire for the shaped course
materialsText: Thick bare metal wire for the shaped course; metal wire loop/handle; insulated handle; low-voltage battery; buzzer; LED and suitable resistor; connecting wires; switch; cardboard or wooden base; tape and pliers
speech: This is a skill game based on an electric circuit. The player moves the metal loop along the shaped wire without touching it. If the loop touches the wire, the circuit is completed and the buzzer or LED gives a signal. The game helps us understand how a switch works and how touching two conductive parts can complete an electric circuit.
note: Use only a low-voltage battery. Cover sharp wire ends and make sure the buzzer and LED are wired correctly.

title: City Model
concept: Urban planning, transport, infrastructure and energy use
materialsText: Large cardboard or foam-board base; small cartons for buildings; coloured paper and paints; road markings; toy cars and train; track or elevated bridge (if included); LEDs for streetlights; wires; low-voltage battery; switches; toy trees; glue; labels
speech: This model represents a city and some of the facilities people use every day. It includes buildings, roads, transport, streetlights and public spaces. A well-planned city needs safe transport, reliable energy, clean water, waste management and green areas. Our model helps us discuss how different parts of a city are connected and how planning can make urban life safer and more sustainable.
note: If the model includes lights or a moving train, demonstrate those features separately and explain which parts are working and which are display models.

title: Working Conveyor Belt
concept: Rotational motion, friction and material handling
materials: rubber belt or wide elastic strip
materialsText: DC geared motor; two rollers; rubber belt or wide elastic strip; wooden or cardboard frame; shafts/axles; pulleys or drive belt; battery holder and batteries; switch; connecting wires; glue or screws; small lightweight objects to transport
speech: This is a small conveyor belt, similar to the systems used in factories, warehouses and airports. A motor turns one roller, which moves the continuous belt around the rollers. Objects placed on the belt are carried from one end to the other. The model demonstrates how rotational motion and friction can be used to transport materials efficiently.
note: Keep fingers, hair and loose clothing away from the rollers and moving belt. Use only lightweight objects.

title: Day and Night Demonstration Model
concept: Earth’s rotation and the cycle of day and night
materials: bright LED lamp or torch to represent the Sun
low-voltage battery and switch for the lamp
optional low-speed motor and holder to rotate the globe
materialsText: Globe or painted foam sphere; bright LED lamp or torch to represent the Sun; stable stands; low-voltage battery and switch for the lamp; optional low-speed motor and holder to rotate the globe; labels; cardboard base
speech: This model explains why we have day and night. The Sun lights up the half of Earth that faces it, while the opposite half is in darkness. Earth rotates on its axis, and different places move into and out of sunlight during this rotation. One complete rotation takes about 24 hours, producing the daily cycle of day and night.
note: Keep the lamp fixed as the Sun and rotate the Earth. Do not move the Sun around Earth for this demonstration.
